species.name: Pink Lemonade
species.photo_note: A regular blue highbush blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum) is shown, not 'Pink Lemonade'.
species.fun_fact: This blueberry was bred in New Jersey, and its berries go from pale green to bright pink as they ripen. It needs far fewer cold winter hours than most blueberries to set fruit, so it crops even after mild winters.
species.uncertain: The plant list just says "Pink Lemonade". This assumes the pink blueberry. Baptisia 'Pink Lemonade' (sold as DECADENCE DELUXE false indigo) is another common plant with the same name.

species.name: Bottlebrush Buckeye
species.fun_fact: It is one of the best summer-flowering shrubs for shade, with foot-long white flower spikes and red-tipped stamens. Missouri Botanical Garden has a large planting along the walk heading south from the Climatron.

species.name: St. Johnswort
species.fun_fact: The genus name means "above a picture", from the old habit of hanging these flowers over images and windows. They were also gathered and burned on the eve of St. John's Day to keep evil spirits away.

credit.author: そらみみ (Soramimi)
credit.file: Flower of hypericum calycinum in Hakozaki Campus, Kyushu University.JPG

species.name: Pretty in Pink Epimedium
species.photo_note: Species shown (Epimedium grandiflorum), not the cultivar.
species.fun_fact: Epimediums are nicknamed bishop's hat and fairy wings for their spurred, airy flowers. The large-flowered species behind 'Pretty in Pink' grows wild in the woodlands of Japan and Korea and blooms in April and May.
species.uncertain: Written as "Pretty & Pink Epimedium". This assumes the cultivar 'Pretty in Pink'.

species.name: Korean Feather Reed Grass
species.fun_fact: In late summer it sends up feathery plumes with a pink tinge, up to about 4 feet tall, that ripen to light tan. Those fluffy seed heads are where the names feather reed grass and foxtail grass come from.

species.name: New Jersey Tea
species.fun_fact: During the Revolutionary War, Americans dried its leaves as a caffeine-free substitute for tea, which is how it got its name. It grows wild in prairies, glades and open woods all over Missouri.

species.name: Girard Azalea
species.photo_note: Shown: 'Girard's Rose', one Girard azalea. The one here may be a different color.
species.fun_fact: Azaleas belong to the genus Rhododendron, Greek for "rose tree". A quick way to tell them apart: true rhododendron flowers have 10 stamens, azaleas have 5.

sources.label: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (Girard's Crimson)

species.uncertain: The plant list does not say which Girard azalea. There are many, such as Girard's Crimson, Fuchsia, Rose and Scarlet.

species.name: Hillside Black Beauty Bugbane
species.fun_fact: The common name bugbane comes from the plant's insect-repelling smell. 'Hillside Black Beauty' has ferny, coppery-purple leaves under tall, fragrant white flower spires in late summer and fall.

species.name: Sugar Shack Buttonbush
species.photo_note: Species shown (Cephalanthus occidentalis), not the cultivar.
species.fun_fact: The round, pincushion-like flower heads are a magnet for bees and butterflies. 'Sugar Shack' is a dwarf form, about 4 feet tall, whose flowers are followed by red, ball-shaped fruit.

species.name: Sweet Woodruff
species.fun_fact: Crushed leaves smell like fresh-cut hay, and the scent gets stronger as they dry, which is why it goes into sachets. It is the traditional flavoring for May wine, a white wine punch.

species.name: Emerald Spreader Yew
species.photo_note: Species shown (Taxus cuspidata), not the cultivar.
species.fun_fact: This Japanese yew creeps slowly outward, reaching about 2.5 feet tall but up to 9 feet wide over 20 years. The red "berries" on female plants are really a fleshy cup, called an aril, around a single seed.

species.name: Lipstick Hosta
species.photo_note: A different gold-leaved hosta is shown, not 'Lipstick'.
species.fun_fact: Hostas are shade-loving perennials from the woodlands of Japan, Korea, China and eastern Russia, grown mostly for their leaves. If this is 'Lipstick Blonde', it was registered in Belgium in 2012 and has golden leaves on purple-red stalks.

sources.label: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (Hosta genus notes)
American Hosta Society Hosta Helper ('Lipstick Blonde')

species.uncertain: No hosta named just 'Lipstick' turned up. The likeliest match is 'Lipstick Blonde' (gold leaves, red stems), or its green-centered sport 'Lipstick Blush'.

species.name: Short-beak Sedge
species.fun_fact: This native sedge likes it dry and sunny, growing wild in prairies, savannas, rock outcrops and dunes. Its chunky seed clusters ripen in June and July on stems up to about 3 feet tall.

credit.author: Matt Lavin from Bozeman, Montana, USA

species.name: Yellowwood
species.fun_fact: The heartwood holds a yellow dye, which gives the tree its name. In late spring a mature tree can be draped in drooping, wisteria-like white flowers, though big bloom years may come only every 2 or 3 years.

credit.author: Rachel White
credit.file: Cladrastis kentukea Yellowwood turning yellow in fall.jpg

species.name: Paperbark Maple
species.fun_fact: Its cinnamon-colored bark peels into curls that stay on the tree instead of falling. Plant hunter E. H. Wilson brought it from China to England in 1899, and Boston's Arnold Arboretum introduced it to the U.S. soon after.

species.name: Espalier or Topiary
species.photo_note: Any tree or shrub trained flat on a wall or clipped into a shape counts. Shown: an espaliered fruit tree.
species.fun_fact: Espalier comes from the Italian spalliera, "something to rest the shoulder against". Ancient Egyptian tomb paintings show fig trees trained this way, and Roman gardeners grew them against walls to stretch the season and get more fruit.

sources.label: UC Marin Master Gardeners (University of California)

species.name: Weeping Tree
species.photo_note: Any tree with a weeping form counts. Shown: a weeping cherry.
species.fun_fact: Many weeping trees are grafted: a weeping top is joined to a straight trunk, often 5 to 6 feet up, which sets the tree's height. Upright shoots that sprout below the graft should be removed.

sources.label: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (weeping cherry)

credit.author: Marty Aligata
credit.file: Pink Weeping Cherry, Cedar Hill Cemetery, Wethersfield, CT - March 27, 2012.jpg

species.name: Elderberry
species.fun_fact: American elder grows wild along streams, woods and fence rows all over Missouri. Its flat clusters of lemon-scented flowers turn into black berries used for jam, pie and elderberry wine.
species.uncertain: Written as "Sambucas". This assumes elderberry (Sambucus), most likely the native American elder. The cultivar is unknown, and it could also be a European elder such as BLACK LACE.

species.name: Cardinal Flower
species.fun_fact: Hummingbirds and butterflies love the flowers, but not cardinals. The name comes from the scarlet robes worn by Roman Catholic cardinals.

credit.author: John Rusk from Berkeley, CA, United States of America

species.name: Thunderhead Japanese Black Pine
species.fun_fact: Japanese black pine is known for whitish buds that stand out against its dark green needles. The species is named for Carl Peter Thunberg, an 18th and 19th century Swedish physician and botanist.

species.name: Arnold Columnar Tulip Tree
species.photo_note: Shown: a tree labeled 'Fastigiatum', the same cultivar under its other name.
species.fun_fact: 'Arnold' is a narrow, columnar tulip tree named for Boston's Arnold Arboretum, and it is the same tree sold as 'Fastigiatum'. The tulip tree is the state tree of Kentucky, Tennessee and Indiana.

species.name: Fireworks Goldenrod
species.fun_fact: Its arching sprays of tiny yellow flowers are said to look like bursting fireworks. Goldenrod gets blamed for hay fever, but the real culprit is wind-blown pollen from plants like ragweed.

species.name: Storm Cloud Bluestar
species.photo_note: Species shown (Amsonia tabernaemontana), not the cultivar.
species.fun_fact: Cut stems ooze a milky sap that helps keep grazing animals away. 'Storm Cloud' starts spring with near-black stems and silver-veined leaves, then opens pale periwinkle-blue star flowers.

species.name: Lemon Purrfection Catmint
species.photo_note: A common blue-flowered catmint (Nepeta × faassenii) is shown, not the gold-leaved cultivar.
species.fun_fact: This compact catmint keeps its bright golden leaves all summer, turning more chartreuse in shade. Lavender-blue flowers start early and keep coming without cutting back.

sources.label: Walters Gardens (the grower that introduced it)

species.uncertain: Written as "Lemon Perfection". The catmint on the market is spelled 'Lemon Purrfection' (Walters Gardens, 2024), so this assumes that one.

species.name: Hummelo Betony
species.fun_fact: The species name officinalis was given to plants sold in apothecary shops for real or supposed medicinal uses. 'Hummelo' sends up dense rose-lavender flower spikes 1.5 to 2 feet tall in summer.
